1.explanation: In Table 1, 2^n mod 11 equals 3 when n = 8 and equals 9 when n = 6, so for blank A Alice's secret is x = 8 and for blank B Bob's secret is y = 6. For blank C the shared key is K = 9^8 mod 11 = 2^48 mod 11; since 2^10 mod 11 = 1, this reduces to 2^8 mod 11 = 3 (Bob gets the same value as 3^6 mod 11 = 3). For blank D, Eve knows R1 = 3 and the stolen y = 3, so she can compute K = R1^y mod p = 27 mod 11 = 5, without needing x. For blank E, a search space of about 2^120 at 2^90 attempts per year takes 2^30 years, which is roughly 1.07 × 10^9, about 1 billion years. This is why Diffie-Hellman relies on a very large prime p: the discrete logarithm has no known efficient solution.

2.explanation: For blank A, address 18 is 000 100 10 in binary, so tag = 000, line = 100 and byte offset = 10; the word starting at address 16 (0A 00 1B 00) is loaded into line 100 with tag 000. For blank B, line 101 with tag 001 gives the address 001 101 00 = 52, so the word holds addresses 52 to 55 (34 to 37 in hex). For blank C, address 0 hits (line 000, tag 000). Address 32 (tag 001, line 000) misses and replaces that line, so address 2 (tag 000) then misses, and address 34 (tag 001) misses again: the remaining sequence is miss → miss. This back-and-forth replacement on the same line is the weakness of a direct-mapped cache. In Table 1, the address range is 0 to 2^(T+L+B) − 1 (blank D, since the full address has T+L+B bits), and the tag storage is 2^L lines × T bits = 2^L × T bits (blank E).

3.explanation: For blank A, each registration belongs to exactly one student, and a student has zero registrations (not yet registered) or one (one topic), so the line is "only one" on the Student side and "zero or one" on the Registration side. For blank B, each registration has exactly one instructor, while an instructor may supervise none or several students (up to 5), so the line is "only one" to "zero or many". For SQL1, blanks C and D are LEFT OUTER JOIN and r.ID IS NULL: the left join keeps every student, and students with no matching registration get NULL registration columns, which picks out S2104 Selena. An inner join would drop exactly the unregistered students you are looking for. For blank E, SQL3 joins each student to their faculty's maximum grade, which is 90 for FIT and 85 for FEE, so three students win: S2102 and S2103 (tied at 90) and S2104.

4.explanation: For blank A, the ARP request is a broadcast and L2SW#1's MAC table is still empty, so the frame arriving on port 1 is flooded to every other port: 2, 3, 4 and 5. Port 5 is the link to the router. Support2 is on a different subnet, so for blanks B, C and D Sales1 sends an ARP request to find the MAC address of the default gateway (192.168.10.1). For blank E, the frame Sales1 sends to Support1 carries the router G0 MAC address 00:00:5E:00:53:AA as its destination MAC, but the destination IP stays Support1's 192.168.20.2. For blank F, when R1 forwards the packet it rewrites the frame header, so Support1 sees source MAC 00:00:5E:00:53:BB (the G1 interface), while the source IP is still Sales1's 192.168.10.2. The key point is that MAC addresses change at each hop and IP addresses stay end-to-end.

5.explanation: For blank A, in test case 1 a = 9 makes (a < 10) true, so (b < 20) is skipped by the short-cut "or"; c = 10 makes (c > 10) false, so (d > 10) is skipped by the short-cut "and". The answer is that b < 20 and d > 10 are not evaluated. For blank B, in test case 2 (a < 10) is false, so b must be checked, and (c > 10) is true, so d must be checked: all single conditions are evaluated. In the control flow graph, node 4 (b < 20) branches to node 5 or to node 6 (func3), so blank C is node 6, and node 7 (c > 10) leads to node 8 (d > 10), so blank D is node 8. For blank E, branch coverage needs 3 test cases: one with x ≤ 10, plus two with x > 10 that together make each inner IF both true and false. For blank F, the graph has 12 nodes (S, 1 to 10, E) and 16 edges, so P = 16 − 12 + 2 = 6.

6.explanation: For blank A, "B" appears at positions 4 and 6 of ACABAB, so its mask has bits 4 and 6 set: 0000000000101000. In Program 1, each mask is first initialized to "0"B (blank B), and then bit i is set for Pat[i] by OR-ing in "1"B << (i − 1) (blank C), because bit 1 is the lowest bit, which needs a shift of 0. For blank D, at i = 2 the status after line α is "11"B, and AND-ing it with A's mask "10101"B gives "1"B. For blanks E and F, Text[9] is "A", so the mask is "10101"B; the status "10"B shifted left and OR-ed with 1 gives "101"B, and AND-ing that with "10101"B leaves "101"B. For blank G, in AC[BA]A[ABC]A each bracket group counts as one position, giving 6 positions. For blank H, the mistaken nested string makes the inner "[" add a position and the following "]" end the mode early, so A's bits land at positions 1, 4, 5 and 7: "1011001"B.

For blank B, malloc must allocate a whole node, so its argument is sizeof(Wrestler_t), not the size of a pointer. For blank C, the first class i with UpperLimits[i] >= weight is the lightest allowed class. In Insert, an empty list gets the node via Entries[i] = wrestler (blank D); otherwise the loop walks to the last node and appends with curr->next = wrestler (blank E). For blank F, Deallocate needs two pointer variables, declared as *curr, *next. For sorted insertion (blank G), the loop continues while curr->next->weight < wrestler->weight. For blank H, line δ (insert at the head) runs for Eric (empty 97 kg list), Faraday (empty 74 kg list) and Issacs (68 is not more than Faraday's 72), so it runs 3 times.

For blank B, add copies a ToDo in only when !todoList.contains(todo), and contains relies on this id-based equals. For blank D, select keeps a ToDo only if every condition holds, so it uses allMatch(c -> c.test(t)) (with no conditions, allMatch is true and every ToDo is returned). For blanks F and G, "Purchase a PC" was never added because update ignores unknown ToDos; all stored ToDos become STARTED; and only HIGH items whose deadline string compares below "20231101" are printed, in insertion order: Send the e-mail (F), then Create the report (G).
